precip.notes: Precipitation rate from GEOS-FP, recovered only where rain colours are visible. Pixels showing clouds, land or ocean count as no rain, so rain under thick cloud is under-counted. Cell value = mean over the 1° cell. Stored log 0.1–20 mm/h; the lowest code (0.1) means dry or ≤0.1 mm/h. The newest steps are short forecasts. Cells under the NASA logo and date label have no data.

pm25.notes: Surface fine particulate matter (PM2.5) from NASA's GEOS-CF composition model, not ground stations. The globe shows the EIC frame's colours (more opaque where the air is dirtier); the numbers come directly from GEOS-CF output at the same hour (analysis, then the latest forecast for the newest hours), because the accuracy test found the frame's colours do not follow its colorbar (values read from the picture were about 4x too low).

tanom.title: GISTEMP v4 surface temperature anomaly (vs 1951–1980)

source.citation: GISTEMP Team, 2026: GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP), version 4. NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies. Dataset accessed 2026-11-05 at https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/. Lenssen, N., G.A. Schmidt, M. Hendrickson, P. Jacobs, M. Menne, and R. Ruedy, 2024: A GISTEMPv4 observational uncertainty ensemble. J. Geophys. Res. Atmos., 129, no. 17, e2023JD040179, doi:10.1029/2023JD040179. Lenssen, N., G. Schmidt, J. Hansen, M. Menne, A. Persin, R. Ruedy, and D. Zyss, 2019: Improvements in the GISTEMP uncertainty model. J. Geophys. Res. Atmos., 124, no. 12, 6307-6326, doi:10.1029/2018JD029522.

time.label: year
time.timing: annual mean of monthly anomalies, Jan–Dec

picture.from: drawn from the GISTEMP values (opacity grows with |anomaly|)

tanom.notes: Values are temperature ANOMALIES in °C relative to the 1951–1980 mean of each grid cell, not absolute temperatures (+1 means 1 °C warmer than that place's 1951–1980 average). Source grid: GISTEMP v4 (GHCN v4 land stations + ERSST v5 sea surface), 2° cells, with each station's influence spread up to 1200 km (1200 km smoothing), so cells far from stations are interpolated. Annual value = mean of the monthly anomalies Jan–Dec; a cell needs at least 9 of 12 months, otherwise it is no data. Years 1880–2025: 2026 is left out because the file (created 2026-10-22) only runs to 2026-09; only complete calendar years are used. Early coverage is sparse: before ~1950 much of the Arctic and Antarctic, the Southern Ocean near the sea ice and parts of Africa and South America are no data, while most ice-free ocean is covered from 1880 because ERSST v5 is itself a statistical reconstruction (share of Earth's area with data — 1880: 83%, 1900: 90%, 1950: 95%, 2025: 99%). Seasonal sea-ice areas can stay no data in recent years too. Stored range -6…+6 °C (uint8 linear); 134 cell-years beyond it are clipped to the end codes. The picture palette (ColorBrewer RdBu, reversed) saturates at ±4 °C: anomalies beyond it are drawn in the end colour but stored up to ±6. Dark grey = no data. series.global is NASA's own global land–ocean annual mean (GLB.Ts+dSST.csv, J-D column), computed by GISS from the full analysis, not an average of these grids.

source.citation: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, Earth Information Center visualization 5313: Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023 - EIC Version (visualizer Kel Elkins, USRA; scientists Zhuosen Wang, Miguel Román, Ranjay Shrestha, Srija Chakraborty, Virginia Kalb). Data: Black Marble: Next Generation, NASA/NOAA Suomi NPP VIIRS. https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5313

time.label: year
time.timing: annual average of night lights, one frame per year in NASA's visualization

picture.from: NASA EIC frame (from NASA's movie of SVS 5313)

lights.notes: Light at night from NASA's Black Marble annual composites (VIIRS on Suomi NPP, NASA/NOAA), read from the EIC visualization SVS 5313, 2012-2023. The picture has no colour scale, so each value is a relative light index 0-100 (100 = a 1-degree cell fully at the picture's brightest), not radiance; compare places and years, not units. The frames come from NASA's movie of the visualization (its frame folder is not public): for each year, the middle frame of the stretch labelled with that year (frames 7, 24, 42, 60, 77, 95, 113, 130, 148, 166, 184, 235); the base map without lights (frame 289) is subtracted. Map position checked against NASA Black Marble 2016: correlation 0.42 at the calibrated position, 0.24 two degrees off. Summed over the globe, the index is +29% in 2023 against 2012.

picture.from: NASA visualization frames (Science On a Sphere copy of SVS 5011)

lightning.notes: Lightning seen by the Lightning Imaging Sensor (LIS) on the International Space Station, read from the EIC visualization SVS 5011 (NASA's Science On a Sphere copy of it, a plain world map with a date for every frame). One frame every 10 days (229 non-overlapping 10-day windows, labelled 11 Mar 2017 to 22 Aug 2023); for each calendar month, the windows labelled in that month are averaged over the years. Each value is the share (0-100 %) of a 1-degree cell covered with NASA's lightning marks: a relative measure, since LIS sees each place for about 90 seconds per pass and the marks have a drawn size. NASA's label file writes 2023 as 2003; those labels come after 31 Dec 2022 and are read as 2023. Checks: map position against NASA Blue Marble, correlation 0.45 (2 degrees off 0.38); 0.00% of marks beyond 58 degrees; 30-50N has 19x more in June-August than December-February, 20-40S 4x more in December-February than June-August.
